To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(a) the oceanic bomb radiocarbon inventory is smaller than previously thought; (b) the oceanic carbon sink is smaller than previously believed; and (c) the oceanic radiocar-bon penetration depth is smaller than previously assumed.
the oceanic uptake of anthropogenic carbon is smaller than previously believed and that the oceanic carbon sink is smaller than believed.

(i) the bomb 14CO2 source strength in the 1960s was at least 25% higher than previously believed, and that (ii) the global oceanic uptake of bomb 13C is therefore 25% smaller than previously believed, which (iii) implies a smaller ocean penetration depth of 14C and a 25% lower estimate for the oceanic uptake of anthropogenic CO2.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the carbon cycle and in particular the oceanic uptake of carbon.
the exchange of carbon between the atmosphere and the ocean.
the exchange of radiocarbon between the atmosphere and the ocean.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the oceans are taking up less carbon than previously thought, but that they are still taking up more than the atmosphere can absorb.
the global ocean takes up about 2.5 Pg C a−1 of anthropogenic CO2.
the oceanic carbon dioxide uptake is smaller than previously thought, and that the oceanic uptake of bomb 13C, which is a tracer for the uptake of fossil CO2, is also smaller than previously thought.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the oceanic carbon dioxide exchange with the atmosphere is smaller than had previously been thought.
the oceans are a smaller carbon sink than previously believed, with an uptake of about 1.6 Pg C yr−1, and that this sink has decreased in recent decades.
the ocean is a less effective carbon sink than was previously believed.
The main takeaway from our work is that
oceanic carbon cycling is not as well constrained by radiocarbon measurements as previously thought.
the oceanic carbon sink may be smaller than previously thought.
the oceanic carbon sink is smaller than previously estimated, and that this is not due to a failure of the carbon cycle model, but to a failure of our understanding of the carbon cycle itself.
